subject: political-science
readings: OD ch. 5 (Orvis & Drogus, *Governing Institutions in Democracies*)

cards.front: State the **red thread** of the whole lecture — the single question every system of government answers, and the master frame you use to place them.
cards.back:
The one question: **how is executive power organised and held accountable?** — i.e. how the executive is *chosen*, *checked*, and *removed*.

**Master frame:** Lijphart's **majoritarian ↔ consensus** continuum, measured by the number of **veto players** (Tsebelis). Westminster parliamentarism = most **majoritarian** (power concentrated, few veto players); US presidentialism = built-in **separation/veto players** (strong horizontal check, gridlock-prone).

Every case: *how is the executive chosen · how removed · how many veto players · what's the accountability/efficiency/stability trade-off?*
cards.hint: Chosen · checked · removed — on Lijphart's line.

cards.front: The **executive** splits into two roles. Name both, and say which one every state must have.
cards.back:
**Head of state** — *symbolic*, represents the country (monarch, ceremonial president).
**Head of government** — runs *policy* (PM, or the president in the US).

One person can hold both (**US president**) or they can be split (**UK monarch + PM**). Only the **executive** is essential to all states; the legislature and judiciary exist to *limit* it. *How these roles relate to the legislature* is what defines the three systems.
cards.hint: Symbolic vs policy; can be one person or two.

cards.front: Define Lijphart's **majoritarian** vs **consensus** democracy — and give the bundle of features that travels with each.
cards.back:
Institutions differ by **how much they concentrate vs disperse power**.

**Majoritarian** (UK): single-party executive, executive dominates the legislature, unicameral, easily amended constitution → **few veto players**.
**Consensus** (US/Germany): coalition executives, executive–legislative balance, bicameral, rigid constitution → **many veto players**.

On Lijphart's map it's not one switch but a *position* on two independent axes: **Executives–Parties** (consensus ↔ majoritarian) and **Federal ↔ Unitary**.
cards.hint: Concentrate vs disperse; few vs many veto players.

cards.front: **Any actor whose agreement is needed to change policy.** Name this concept, name its theorist, and state the rule about adding more of them.
cards.back:
**Veto player** — **Tsebelis**.

**Rule:** the more veto players (and the greater the *ideological distance* between them), the **less policy change** — smaller winset, more gridlock. It's the mechanism behind presidential gridlock *and* the stability of consensus systems.
cards.hint: Tsebelis; more of them → less change.

cards.front: Walk through the **veto-players / winset** diagram: how does a new policy pass, and what happens as you add players A → B → C?
cards.back:
Each circle = one player's set of policies it prefers to the **status quo (SQ)**. A new policy passes only if it lies inside **every** player's circle — the **overlap (winset)**.

**One player** → winset is huge (all of A). **Add B** → shrinks to the small hatched sliver (AB). **Add C** → it can vanish entirely.

**Take-away:** more veto players + more ideological distance → **smaller winset → less policy change / gridlock.**
cards.hint: Policy must sit inside every circle at once.

cards.front: **Citizens punish the government at the ballot box vs the courts strike down a law passed by the legislature.** Name the two *types of accountability*, who coined the pair, and which one this chapter is about.
cards.back:
**Vertical accountability** — *citizens → state* (elections; ch. 6).
**Horizontal accountability** — *state institutions check each other* (this chapter).

Both from **O'Donnell**. Ballot-box = vertical; courts striking a law = horizontal.

Use them to *evaluate* a system: parliamentarism = clearest **vertical** (voters know whom to blame) but weak **horizontal**; presidentialism = strong **horizontal** (separation) but can hurt policymaking.
cards.hint: Citizens→state vs state→state; O'Donnell.

cards.front: Define **parliamentarism** (Westminster) — the defining relationship, who the PM is, and where it sits on Lijphart's line.
cards.back:
Executive and legislature are **fused**: parliament elects the chief executive (**PM**), who is *both* the majority-party leader *and* a sitting legislator. The purest **majoritarian** form.

**PM is not directly elected** — citizens vote for parliament; the majority names the PM. A **ceremonial head of state** (monarch, or esteemed elected president) stays out of politics.

With a disciplined single majority the PM is *"the most powerful democratic executive in the world"* — legislation passes almost automatically.
cards.hint: Fusion; PM = party leader + MP; not directly elected.

cards.front: Run the **removal mechanism in parliamentarism**: how is a PM taken out, and what are the PM's counter-moves?
cards.back:
**Vote of no confidence** → the PM resigns (party picks a new leader) *or* asks the head of state to call **new elections**.

**PM's counter-move:** can **dissolve** parliament and trigger elections. Usually **no fixed terms**.

No-confidence votes succeed only **~5% of the time**, but even losing one signals fatal weakness. *(UK: 117 of May's own MPs voted no-confidence; she resigned.)*
cards.hint: No confidence → resign or new elections; PM can dissolve.

cards.front: Define **presidentialism** — the defining feature (and whose idea it traces to), plus how it builds in veto players.
cards.back:
Executive and legislature are **elected separately with separate powers** — **separation of powers** (**Montesquieu**). The defining feature is *separation*, **not** that one person is both head of state and government.

**President is directly elected**, serves a **fixed term**; branches generally **can't remove each other**. Lawmaking needs *both* president *and* legislative majority → **institutional veto players** → checks & balances, but **gridlock** (esp. under divided government).

The **legislature is typically more powerful** than in parliamentary systems.
cards.hint: Separation (Montesquieu); directly elected; fixed term.

cards.front: In **presidentialism**, why is it so hard to remove the executive, and why does policymaking stall? Trace the chain.
cards.back:
**Removal:** branches can't sack each other — the only route is a hard **impeachment**; the president holds a **fixed term** regardless of support.

**Policy chain:** separation of powers → lawmaking needs *both* president and legislative majority → these are **built-in veto players** → under **divided government** neither can force the other → **gridlock** (e.g. US Senate's 60-vote filibuster).

**Samuels:** presidential systems **change the status quo less and more slowly** (*Thatcher reshaped economic policy far more than Reagan*).
cards.hint: Fixed term + impeachment only; two elected veto players.

cards.front: Define **semi-presidentialism** — how executive power is arranged, and where/when it originated.
cards.back:
Executive power is **split** between a **directly elected president** (head of state, with *real* powers) and a **PM** (head of government, backed by the parliamentary majority, appointed by the president, removable by no-confidence).

Legislation needs the president's signature **and** PM/majority support; powers must be **clearly divided** (often unclear in practice).

Originated in **France, 1958 (de Gaulle)** — the Fifth Republic. Spread from **10 systems (1990) → 52 (2018)**.
cards.hint: Split executive: elected president + PM; France 1958.

cards.front: Explain **cohabitation** — when it happens, what the president must do, and why France shows it *working*.
cards.back:
**Cohabitation** = president and legislative majority from **different parties**. The president must appoint a **PM from the opposing majority** and retreat to their own domain (French norm: **president runs foreign policy & defence, PM runs domestic**).

It works precisely *because* the president **cannot simply dismiss the PM** — so the two share power and the system stays **as stable as parliamentarism** (Mitterrand with a right-wing PM; Chirac with a left-wing PM).

Limits presidential power but can cause gridlock.
cards.hint: President + majority from different parties → opposing-party PM.

cards.front: **One question decides whether a semi-presidential system is safe or dangerous for democracy.** Name the question, its theorist, and the two outcomes.
cards.back:
**Elgie's key question:** *can the president dismiss the PM?*

**If YES →** unstable, democracy endangered — the president has no incentive to compromise (**Russia**).
**If NO →** genuine power-sharing, **no less stable than parliamentarism** (**France**).

France vs Russia are the mirror images that sit on either side of Elgie's dividing line.
cards.hint: Can the president fire the PM? Russia yes, France no.

cards.front: The **core comparison** — for **parliamentary / presidential / semi-presidential**, contrast: powers · how the executive is chosen · terms · how it's removed · veto players.
cards.back:
**Powers:** fused / separated / split executive.
**Head of state & govt:** separate (monarch + **PM**) / **same person** (president) / president (HoS) + **PM** (HoG).
**Chosen by:** **parliament** names PM / **directly elected** / president direct + PM by parliament.
**Terms:** usually **none** / **fixed** / fixed presidential term + PM on parliament.
**Removed by:** **no confidence** (+ dissolution) / **impeachment** only / PM by no-confidence, president fixed.
**Veto players:** few / built-in / depends (cohabitation adds them).
**Cases:** UK, Germany, India / USA, Brazil / France, Russia.
cards.hint: Fused · separated · split — learn the row for each.

cards.front: These features → **which system?** Powers *fused*; executive from the legislature; chief executive is a sitting legislator + party leader; removed by no-confidence; usually no fixed term.
cards.back:
**Parliamentarism** (Westminster).

Giveaways: **fusion** of powers, the executive *sits in* the legislature, removal by **vote of no confidence** (+ dissolution), **no fixed term**. Classic cases: **UK, Germany, India**. The purest **majoritarian** form — **few veto players**.
cards.hint: Fusion + no-confidence + no fixed term.

cards.front: These features → **which system?** Powers *separated*; head of state and head of government are the **same directly-elected person**; fixed term; removal only by impeachment; branches can't sack each other.
cards.back:
**Presidentialism.**

Giveaways: **separation of powers** (Montesquieu), one directly-elected person is *both* HoS and HoG, **fixed term**, **impeachment** as the only removal, **built-in veto players** and gridlock. Classic cases: **USA, Brazil**. Note the paradox: the **legislature is more powerful** here than under parliamentarism.
cards.hint: Separation + same person + fixed term + impeachment.

cards.front: These features → **which system?** A directly-elected president *with real powers* **plus** a PM answerable to parliament; the president appoints the PM but the PM can fall to no-confidence; cohabitation is possible.
cards.back:
**Semi-presidentialism** (the hybrid / split executive).

Giveaways: **two-headed executive** — elected president (HoS, real power) + PM (HoG) backed by the majority; **cohabitation** when they're from different parties; **Elgie's test** (can the president dismiss the PM?) decides stability. Classic cases: **France, Russia**. Born France 1958.
cards.hint: Elected president WITH powers + a PM = two heads.

cards.front: Counter-intuitive claim: the **legislature is *more* powerful in presidential systems** than in parliamentary ones. Explain the mechanism.
cards.back:
Under **separation of powers**, a legislator **can't also sit in the cabinet** — so members have **no ministerial promotion to earn** from the executive and stay **independent**.

In a **parliamentary** system, ministers *are* MPs, so ambitious MPs **toe the party line** to be promoted into the cabinet → a weaker, executive-dependent legislature.

(Note: this is about chasing **cabinet posts**, not re-election — every legislator chases their own seat.)
cards.hint: Can a legislator become a minister? That's the lever.

cards.front: **"Presidentialism is inherently crisis-prone"** — name the theorist, the famous article, and the **three perils**.
cards.back:
**Linz (1990), "The Perils of Presidentialism."**

**① Dual legitimacy** — two independently elected branches, *no democratic tie-breaker.*
**② Winner-take-all** — presidents over-read their mandate and won't compromise.
**③ Inflexible fixed terms** — a failing president can't be removed.

Danger peaks for **new democracies** under **coalitional presidentialism** (small presidential party + fragmented legislature — see **Brazil**).
cards.hint: Linz 1990; dual legitimacy · winner-take-all · fixed terms.

cards.front: How does **Cheibub (2007)** rebut Linz — and what does the evidence say about semi-presidentialism's stability?
cards.back:
**Cheibub's counter:** it's not the *institution* but the *society*. Presidential systems just *"tend to exist in societies where democracies of any type are likely to be unstable."* The correlation is spurious.

And **semi-presidentialism is empirically no less stable than parliamentarism** — *provided* the president **can't override the legislature or sack the PM** (echoing **Elgie**).

This is the set-piece **stability debate**: Linz (institution is the culprit) vs Cheibub (society is).
cards.hint: Society, not institution; selection effect.

cards.front: Contrast **common law** and **code law** — their origin, how judges treat precedent, and the *type of judicial review* each produces.
cards.back:
**Common law** (Britain + colonies incl. US): judges **follow precedent** → **decentralised + concrete** review — *any* court can rule on constitutionality, but only inside a real case.

**Code law** (Roman/**Napoleon**; French/Iberian colonies): a written **code** is supreme, **precedent ignored** → **centralised + abstract** review — one special **constitutional court** can rule on a law *in the abstract*.

The split tracks **colonial heritage** (OD Map 5.2).
cards.hint: Precedent → decentralised/concrete; code → centralised/abstract.

cards.front: Define **judicial review**, explain why it's controversial, and name the trend of courts entering ever more political fights.
cards.back:
**Judicial review** = courts can strike down a law as **unconstitutional** → making the judiciary a **veto player** and a check on the majority.

**The controversy:** *why should unelected judges override elected majorities?* Defenders (Dahl 1957): legislatures aren't perfectly representative either; judges are **appointed by elected officials** and sit within the ruling coalition; courts *claim* to protect minorities (though studies find they more often side with the powerful). Only real if **institutionalised** + backed by hard-won **legitimacy** (courts command neither army nor purse).

**Trend:** the **"judicialisation of politics"** (**Tate & Vallinder**) — courts pulled into more and more political questions.
cards.hint: Strike laws down; the 'unelected judges' problem; Tate & Vallinder.

cards.front: Why does a professional bureaucracy create a **principal–agent problem** — and what makes it *worse*? Trace it.
cards.back:
**Professionalisation** (merit appointment) replaced **patronage** and gives bureaucrats **expertise = their own independent power** → the gap: **agents** (officials) pursue their *own* interests, not the **principal's** (elected leaders / public) → inefficiency or corruption (expanding budgets/turf, taking bribes).

**Controls** (all imperfect): political appointees, specific legislation, **legislative oversight**, courts. **New Public Management (NPM)** (Reagan/Thatcher) tried markets — a UK study found a **1/3 staff cut but slightly *higher* costs and *worse* service.**
cards.hint: Expertise = independent power = the gap; controls all leak.

cards.front: Name each: (a) a closed policy loop of bureaucrats + legislators + business serving insiders; (b) Japanese officials taking jobs in firms they'd regulated; (c) the 1980s reform importing markets and "customer satisfaction" into government.
cards.back:
(a) **Iron triangle** — the cosy, closed loop that keeps outsiders out.
(b) ***Amakudari*** — "descent from heaven" (the **Japan** bureaucracy case).
(c) **New Public Management (NPM)** — privatise, add competition, flatten hierarchies (Reagan/Thatcher).

All three are ways unelected **bureaucratic power** operates or gets reined in.
cards.hint: Triangle · heaven-descent · Reagan/Thatcher reform.

cards.front: Contrast **unitary** and **federal** systems — where sovereignty sits, and why federalism is a majority-limiting device.
cards.back:
**Unitary** (France, UK, **Denmark**): the centre holds **sole sovereignty**; local powers are **delegated & revocable**.
**Federal** (US, Germany): sovereignty is **constitutionally shared** with subunits — a built-in way to **limit majorities and protect minorities** (more veto players).

**But federalism is only as real as the politics behind it** — real power depends on **revenue control** and **upper-house strength**, not paper (strong **US Senate** vs weak German **Bundesrat**; **Mexico's** PRI centralised a paper-federal state; **Russia** = a federal *shell*).
cards.hint: Sole vs shared sovereignty; revenue + upper house = the reality test.

cards.front: Name each federalism term: (a) all subunits have equal powers; (b) some subunits get special powers; (c) reversible decentralisation *within a unitary state*.
cards.back:
(a) **Symmetrical** federalism (US).
(b) **Asymmetrical** federalism (special powers for some units).
(c) **Devolution** — reversible decentralisation in a **unitary** state (UK → Scotland/Wales/N. Ireland).

Bonus: **Riker** — federalism is inherently **unstable**, tending toward either centralisation or secession.
cards.hint: Equal · special · reversible-within-unitary.

cards.front: **Rules ≠ outcomes.** Give the two go-to illustrations that the *party system* (not the paper constitution) drives how a government actually works.
cards.back:
**① UK vs India (same Westminster rules):** a disciplined UK majority makes the PM *"the most powerful executive in the world"*; India copied the model but its **party system** decides — one-party Congress dominance (1947–89) made PMs *less* constrained, while post-1989 **coalitions** forced constant bargaining (**3 PMs in 30 years → 12 in the next 30**).

**② Thatcher vs Reagan (Samuels):** with a compliant majority **Thatcher reshaped economic policy far more than Reagan**, who faced a Democratic Congress — despite similar aims.

**Lesson:** context — party number & discipline — turns the *same* rules into different outcomes.
cards.hint: UK vs India; Thatcher vs Reagan.

cards.front: Match each **case** to its system and its one-line lesson: **USA · Brazil · France · Russia · Japan.**
cards.back:
**USA** — **presidential**: separation of powers + weak, polarised parties → **gridlock**; the world's strongest legislature.
**Brazil** — **coalitional presidentialism**: strong *formal* powers ≠ effective power (~30 parties → 9-party coalitions; Rousseff impeached 2016) — the instability Linz warned of.
**France** — **semi-presidential** done *right*: cohabitation works because the president **can't** sack the PM.
**Russia** — **semi-presidential** gone dominant: a president who *can* remove the PM → **electoral authoritarianism** (Elgie's warning).
**Japan** — the **bureaucracy** case: unelected power via **iron triangles** + *amakudari* (principal–agent).
cards.hint: US=gridlock · Brazil=coalitional · France=cohabitation · Russia=dominant · Japan=bureaucracy.

cards.front: **Iversen & Soskice (2006):** why do **proportional** democracies redistribute *more* than **majoritarian** ones? Run the three-class logic.
cards.back:
With three classes (lower / middle / upper):

**Proportional system →** the **middle class sides with the lower class** to redistribute from the rich → **bigger welfare states**.
**Majoritarian system →** the **middle class sides with the upper class** to avoid heavy taxes from the poor → **less redistribution**.

So the majoritarian/PR *institutional* choice has huge distributional stakes — a bridge to Lecture 5 and a big reason PR democracies redistribute more (helps explain the Sweden-vs-US welfare puzzle).
cards.hint: Which class does the middle class ally with?

cards.front: You're handed *any* country and asked to classify and evaluate its system of government. What's the **reusable 4-step template**?
cards.back:
**① How is the executive chosen?** — parliament names it (parliamentary) · directly elected & same person (presidential) · elected president + separate PM (semi-presidential).
**② How is it removed?** — no-confidence + dissolution / impeachment only / mixed.
**③ How many veto players?** — place it on Lijphart's **majoritarian ↔ consensus** line (check party system + federalism).
**④ What's the trade-off?** — read **vertical vs horizontal accountability**, effective policymaking, and stability (deploy **Linz vs Cheibub**).

Always add: *rules ≠ outcomes* — the **party system** decides how the rules actually bite.
cards.hint: Chosen → removed → veto players → trade-off.
